method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Consider a serious eye injury in any child with a painful eye or blurred vision.**
claims.source_text: Consider a serious eye injury when a child presents with a painful eye or blurred vision
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Sight-threatening:** ruptured globe · retrobulbar haematoma · intraocular or corneal foreign body · large hyphaema · retinal detachment · chemical or thermal corneal burn. **Alkalis penetrate deeper** and can burn later.
claims.source_text: The following traumatic conditions threaten vision: Ruptured globe Retrobulbar haematoma Foreign body, either intraocular or corneal Large hyphaemas (causing acute glaucoma) Retinal detachment Corneal burns, either chemical or thermal alkalis penetrate deeper and have greater potential for serious injury and delayed burns
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ask about high-velocity projectiles or chemicals** — air guns, lawn mowers, power tools, hammering, motor vehicle accidents.
claims.source_text: Proximity to chemicals or high velocity projectiles (particularly air guns, lawn mowers, power tools, hammering or motor vehicle accidents)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Signs of globe rupture or laceration:** severe loss of vision or red reflex · loss of ocular motility · asymmetric irregular pupil · hyphaema · distorted globe · localised conjunctival haemorrhage or chemosis.
claims.source_text: Assess for globe rupture or laceration: Severe loss of vision or loss of red reflex Loss of ocular motility Asymmetric, irregular pupil Hyphaema Distorted appearance of globe Localised conjunctival haemorrhage or chemosis (bulging of the conjunctiva)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Manage life-threatening injuries first**, and consider head and C-spine injury before the eye.
claims.source_text: Assessment and management of eye trauma should occur after management of other life-threatening injuries and consideration of head and C-spine injury
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Give adequate analgesia**; the younger child may need procedural sedation. **Get senior or ophthalmology help early** if a distressed child cannot be examined.
claims.source_text: Adequate analgesia will aid examination and procedural sedation may be required in the younger child … Seek senior clinician or ophthalmology assistance early if eye assessment is proving difficult in the distressed child
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Topical tetracaine 0.5% or 1%:** one drop anaesthetises after 20 seconds and lasts 10–20 minutes (longer with 1%). ⚠️ **Do not repeat doses** — epithelial toxicity delays corneal healing.
claims.source_text: Topical anaesthetic such as tetracaine (amethocaine) 0.5% or 1% can be used to assist with examination … One drop into the affected eye will induce anaesthesia after 20 seconds and the effect lasts 10 - 20 minutes (longer with 1%) … Avoid repeated administration of anaesthetic eye drops due to direct epithelial toxicity that can delay corneal healing
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Urgent, copious irrigation after topical anaesthetic, including under the top lid.** Sedation or urgent GA may be needed; remove particulate alkali completely with a cotton bud.
claims.source_text: Urgent, copious irrigation, after local topical anaesthetic, including under top lid. Sedation or urgent GA may be required … Particulate alkaline matter needs urgent, total removal with a cotton bud
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Irrigate with 3 litres of 0.9% sodium chloride through an open giving set over about 15 minutes**, from 3–5 cm above the eye, while the child looks in each direction.
claims.source_text: Use 3 litres of 0.9% sodium chloride through an open giving set over about 15 minutes … Irrigate from 3-5 cm above the ocular surface. Ask the child to look left, right, up and down whilst irrigating
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Continue until conjunctival pH is normal (6–8)** on universal indicator paper. **Discuss every eye burn with ophthalmology.**
claims.source_text: Continue irrigation until pH normal (6-8). Measure pH using universal indicator paper in the conjunctival fornix … Discuss all burns with the ophthalmologist
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Thermal burns: first aid comes before a complete examination** — local anaesthetic and copious irrigation.
claims.source_text: Thermal burns First aid takes precedence over a complete examination Local anaesthetic and copious irrigation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refer to ophthalmology** embedded or metallic foreign bodies (do not remove them) and large, deep or central corneal foreign bodies. ⚠️ **A defect over 2 mm or deep: presume full thickness and manage as penetrating.**
claims.source_text: Seek ophthalmology advice and removal of: Embedded or metallic foreign bodies and avoid removing Large, deep, or central corneal foreign bodies … If large (>2mm) or deep defect seen, presume full thickness abrasion and manage as per penetrating eye injury
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Anaesthetise, evert the lids and stain with fluorescein**; remove a small foreign body with a moistened cotton bud (a 25 gauge needle, bevel up, only in older cooperative children at the slit lamp).
claims.source_text: Anaesthetise conjunctiva with one drop tetracaine (amethocaine) 1% or oxybuprocaine (benoxinate) 0.4% … Examine surface of eye and under lids by everting the eyelids … Stain with fluorescein to assess for corneal abrasion … Remove small foreign body with moistened cotton bud. A 25 gauge needle with bevel up may be used in older, cooperative children, using slit lamp
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Defect over 2 mm:** chloramphenicol 1% ointment and double eye-pad overnight. **Under 2 mm:** chloramphenicol 0.5% drops four times a day for 5 to 7 days.
claims.source_text: For larger defects (>2 mm) apply chloramphenicol 1% ointment and double eye-pad overnight … <2 mm) apply chloramphenicol 0.5% drops four times per day for 5 to 7 days
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Review daily** (visual acuity and slit lamp) until healed; **pain beyond 48 hours or no improvement → ophthalmology.**
claims.source_text: Need daily review (visual acuity and slit lamp examination) until epithelium healed … For persistent pain (>48 hours) or no improvement, seek ophthalmology advice
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Contact lens red eye:** remove the lens, stain, swab any discharge — **Gram-negatives including *P. aeruginosa* are frequent**, so broader cover is needed. **Ulcer → urgent ophthalmology.** Start topical chloramphenicol (1% ointment or 0.5% drops) and arrange follow-up.
claims.source_text: Anaesthetise eye and remove contact lenses if possible … Stain eye and check for corneal abrasions or foreign body … Swab if discharge present, Gram-negatives including P. aeruginosa are frequently the cause, thus requiring broader-spectrum antibiotics … If ulcer identified refer urgently to ophthalmology … Start topical chloramphenicol (1% ointment or 0.5% drops) and arrange for follow-up
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Retrobulbar haematoma** — tense proptosis, limited eye movements, reduced acuity, RAPD: **emergent ophthalmology referral; may need urgent decompression.**
claims.source_text: Retrobulbar haematoma Occurs due to blunt trauma leading to compartment syndrome and optic nerve compression Tense proptosis, limited eye movements, decreased visual acuity and Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) Emergent ophthalmology referral, may require urgent decompression
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Orbital blow-out fracture** (pain, diplopia especially on upward gaze, cheek numbness, lid crepitus): **CT orbit and ophthalmology/maxillofacial referral.**
claims.source_text: Orbital blow out fracture Occurs due to high energy blunt trauma that increases intra-orbital pressure Symptoms include pain and diplopia (particularly on upward gaze), tenderness, eyelid swelling, nausea, and vomiting … Signs can include ptosis, tenderness, relative enophthalmos, decreased sensation of cheek, lower eye lid crepitus … CT of the orbit and ophthalmology/maxillofacial surgery referral
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Treat a lid laceration as penetrating until proven otherwise.** Superficial ones away from the margin can be sutured; **any lid-margin laceration is repaired by an ophthalmologist.**
claims.source_text: Lid laceration Treat as a potential penetrating injury until proven otherwise … Superficial laceration away from the lid margin, may be safely closed by standard suture techniques … Any laceration that involves the eye lid margin should be repaired by an ophthalmologist
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Subconjunctival haemorrhage:** localised may mean penetration; if its posterior edge cannot be seen, consider orbital or base-of-skull fracture; **in infants it may signal non-accidental injury.**
claims.source_text: If localised, may suggest penetrating injury (but can be due to Valsalva manoeuvre) … If the posterior extent of the haemorrhage cannot be visualised, an orbital or base of skull fracture is possible … In infants, subconjunctival haemorrhage may be a sign of non-accidental injury
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consult ophthalmology for** a sight-threatening condition · a large or hard-to-remove corneal foreign body · a distressed child who needs examination · retinal photography for suspected abuse.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with ophthalmology: A child with: A sight threatening condition A large corneal foreign body, or one that is difficult to remove If required to facilitate a complete examination particularly in distressed child If retinal assessment and photography is required for suspected child abuse
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge when** the eye examination is normal, **or** sight-threatening conditions are excluded **and** minor injuries are treated **and** follow-up or early-review criteria are given.
claims.source_text: Consider discharge when Normal eye examination and nil other symptoms or Sight threatening conditions are excluded AND Appropriate treatment instituted for minor injuries AND Follow up, or early review criteria provided to child and family
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Acute eye injury' (Last updated October 2022), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_eye_injury/, retrieved 2026-09-23
